items.feature: Topic versus object particles and SOV order

corpusAnchor.note: Subject–Object–Verb: 'I water drink.' The 을 on 물 is a tag that says 'this is the thing being acted on' — which is why Korean can shuffle words and still make sense.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept a natural polite declarative such as 저는 물을 마셔요. A dropped topic is acceptable if the first-person meaning remains clear; 물 must remain the object of drinking.

items.feature: Volitional negation 안 versus inability 못

corpusAnchor.note: Negation is one tiny word: 안 sits directly before the verb. No do-support, no word-order gymnastics — 안 먹어요, done.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept a natural polite refusal or habitual non-eating such as 저는 고기를 안 먹어요 or 저는 고기를 먹지 않아요. 못 먹어요 alone changes the meaning to inability and is not acceptable.

corpusAnchor.note: The -(으)시- honorific hides inside 오세요 (오 + 시 + 어요). It elevates the SUBJECT — you use it about respected people, never about yourself.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept 선생님이 오세요 or another natural polite rendering that honors the teacher as subject. A request telling the teacher to come or a claim that the speaker comes reverses the role.

corpusAnchor.note: No 'my' needed — whose hands would they be? Korean drops possessives the way it drops subjects: anything obvious goes unsaid.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept 손을 씻어요 with the speaker and ownership understood, or a natural polite form with an explicit first-person topic. Do not require a literal possessive on hands.

items.feature: 밥 literal rice versus ordinary meal/food reading

corpusAnchor.note: 밥 is literally cooked rice but stands in for food and meals in general — eating 밥 just means eating.

items.acceptableAnswerNote: Accept 저는 밥을 먹어요 or another natural polite rendering meaning that the speaker eats food or a meal. 밥 may be explained literally as cooked rice, but the answer must not assert that only rice is eaten.

corpusAnchor.note: Same skeleton with a different subject: 가 marks 친구 as the do-er, 를 marks 커피 as the thing liked, verb caps it off.
The 없어요 pattern from Module 1, mid-recipe: 'sugar not-exists' = we're out of sugar.
-(으)세요's second job: a polite request TO you (Module 4 used it as a statement ABOUT elders — same ending, context decides; the gap deck sorts it).
Your first past tense: 만나다 → drop 다, last vowel is ㅏ so add 았어요 → 만났어요. The subject is understood and simply dropped.

items.feature: 맛있다 literal taste-exists versus delicious reading

corpusAnchor.note: 맛있다 is literally 맛 (taste) + 있다 (exists) — 'taste exists.' Describing words are verbs in Korean, so no 'is' is needed.
